data: Kourou's first launch site: Europa II, Ariane 1 and Giotto on this ground, rebuilt in 2001 for Vega and Vega-C

The Vega launch complex (ELV, also called ZLV or SLV) stands on the site of Kourou's first launch base: built as BEC for the Europa II (one flight, 5 November 1971, failed), rebuilt as ELA-1 for Ariane 1 (first flight 24 December 1979), Ariane 2 and Ariane 3 (last flight 11 July 1989), and from November 2001 rebuilt again for Vega, keeping the Ariane 1 flame trench. Vega first flew from it on 13 February 2012 and Vega-C on 13 July 2022; Wikipedia counts 56 launches from the site by September 2026. Sources: Wikipedia (Ensemble de Lancement Vega launch tables), ESA (Vega and Vega-C pages); coordinates from Wikipedia and OpenStreetMap.

Three launch bases have stood on this spot at Kourou. Europe built the first for the Europa II, whose only flight on 5 November 1971 failed. Rebuilt as ELA-1, it flew Ariane 1 from 24 December 1979, then Ariane 2 and 3 until 11 July 1989. Giotto left from here on an Ariane 1 on 2 July 1985 to meet Halley's Comet. From November 2001 the pad was rebuilt for Vega, keeping the Ariane 1 flame trench and adding a 50 m retractable assembly building. Vega first flew on 13 February 2012, Vega-C on 13 July 2022. Payloads include LISA Pathfinder, Sentinel-2A and 2B, ADM-Aeolus and BIOMASS. Wikipedia counts 56 launches from the site by September 2026, 22 of them Vega and 8 Vega-C. The tower sits close to the equator at 5.2 degrees north.
ESA's first deep-space mission; closest comet flyby ever attempted (Halley, 596 km, 1986); first close-up imaging of a cometary nucleus
Europe's first independent orbital launcher — opened the commercial-comsat era for ESA, flew Giotto to Halley
First close-up images of a cometary nucleus — flew 596 km past Halley's Comet at 68 km/s in 1986
Ariane 5's home pad — JWST + Galileo + a quarter of geostationary commercial sats over a decade
Europe's Soyuz pad: first Soyuz outside Baikonur or Plesetsk (2011), 27 launches, eight for Galileo
Ariane 6's home pad — Europe's geostationary access after Ariane 5
Apollo 10 + Skylab + 53 Shuttle flights; now NASA's SLS / Artemis pad
Plesetsk's workhorse Soyuz pad at 62.9°N — the world's highest-latitude active orbital launch complex
Launched Apollo 8, 9 and 11–17 (Apollo 9 in Earth orbit; Apollo 10 flew from 39B); today flies Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, and Crew Dragon
